chapters.title: Commodity Markets in India — Structure and Players

lessons.title: India's Commodity Exchanges — MCX, NCDEX, and SEBI's Regulatory Role

children.text: On 31 July 2013, the National Spot Exchange Limited (NSEL) suspended trading in most of its contracts. Thousands of investors had put money into what looked like short-term commodity trades, believing their positions were backed by real stock sitting in exchange-certified warehouses. When the exchange stopped paying, an eventual default of about ₹5,600 crore came to light, and investigations found that warehouse stocks had been wildly overstated or simply did not exist. NSEL was not a futures exchange, and it was not regulated by the same rulebook as MCX or NCDEX. That gap is exactly why this lesson exists: you need to know what a properly regulated commodity derivatives exchange actually guarantees, and what it does not.

body.text: A regulated commodity derivatives exchange does three things a random trading platform does not: it standardises every contract, it guarantees settlement through a clearing corporation regardless of whether your counterparty pays, and it operates under a regulator, SEBI, that sets the rules on membership, margins and market conduct.

children.text: Two Exchanges, Two Specialities: MCX and NCDEX

India has two commodity derivatives exchanges that matter for a retail or HNI investor. Both were incorporated in 2003, both are demutualised (meaning ownership and trading rights are separated, so no single broker controls the exchange), and both are regulated by SEBI. Where they differ is what trades on them.

cells: Gold, silver, crude oil, natural gas, copper, zinc, aluminium
Chana, guar seed and guar gum, soybean, mustard seed, cotton, castor seed
Where prices tend to take their cue
Global benchmarks such as COMEX gold and NYMEX crude, adjusted for the rupee
Domestic supply, mandi arrivals, and the monsoon
Jewellers, refiners, oil marketing companies, import-dependent manufacturers
Farmer producer organisations, food processors, exporters of agri commodities
Yes, MCX shares trade on the NSE and BSE
No, NCDEX is not itself a listed company as of this writing

body.text: You do not need a separate account for each exchange. A single commodity trading account with a SEBI-registered broker, such as Zerodha or any full-service broker, typically gives you access to both MCX and NCDEX contracts, alongside your regular equity account.

children.text: The Clearing Corporation: Nobody Trades With a Stranger

markDefs.definition: The exchange practice of inserting itself between every buyer and seller, becoming the legal counterparty to both, so neither side is exposed to the other's default.

children.text: The previous lesson mentioned that futures remove counterparty risk. Here is how. The moment your buy order matches a sell order on MCX or NCDEX, the exchange's clearing corporation steps in through a process called
novation

: it becomes the seller to you, the buyer, and the buyer to whoever sold. You are never actually exposed to the person on the other side of your trade again. If they vanish tomorrow, the clearing corporation still owes you, because it collects margin from both sides upfront and marks every position to market daily, precisely to make sure it never gets caught out. Chapter 2 walks through this in full detail.

body.title: Who guarantees your futures trade?
body.question: You buy one lot of MCX crude oil futures. The person who originally sold that contract defaults and cannot pay. What happens to your position?
options: You lose your entire position, since your counterparty defaulted
You must find a new counterparty yourself before the exchange will honour the contract
Nothing changes for you, because the clearing corporation was already your legal counterparty, not the original seller
The exchange cancels all trades from that day
body.explanation: Novation means the clearing corporation, not the other trader, is your actual counterparty from the moment your trade is matched. Its default is the clearing corporation's problem to manage through the defaulter's margin and its own default fund, not yours.

children.text: What Went Wrong at NSEL, and Why the Whole System Changed

NSEL was launched in 2008 as a spot exchange, meant only for trades that settle almost immediately, backed by commodities genuinely sitting in a warehouse. Instead, it allowed pairs of contracts, an immediate buy leg and a longer-dated sell leg, that behaved like unregulated financing arrangements rather than genuine spot trades in warehouse-verified stock. Because it was licensed as a spot exchange, it fell outside the FMC's derivatives oversight, and nobody was independently confirming that the warehouse receipts backing these trades were real.

events.title: NSEL launches
events.description: Promoted by Financial Technologies (the same group that promoted MCX), NSEL begins operating as India's first electronic spot exchange for commodities.

events.title: Trading suspended
events.description: NSEL suspends trading in most contracts after the government directs it to stop launching new paired contracts. It becomes clear the exchange cannot pay investors.

events.title: The default and the investigation
events.description: An eventual default of about ₹5,600 crore comes to light. Investigations find warehouse stocks were overstated or missing, and that the exchange's paired-contract structure amounted to unregulated financing dressed up as spot commodity trading.

events.title: Consequences for the promoter
events.description: Regulators find Financial Technologies (later renamed 63 Moons Technologies) unfit to continue holding a controlling stake in a regulated exchange, and it exits its shareholding in MCX in the years that follow.

events.title: FMC merges into SEBI
events.description: The push for a single, stronger commodities regulator, already under discussion for years, gains urgency after NSEL, and the FMC is formally merged into SEBI.

body.title: A spot exchange like NSEL vs a derivatives exchange like MCX or NCDEX

columns.label: Spot exchange (the NSEL model)
points: Meant for near-immediate settlement against real, verified stock
No exchange-wide margining or daily mark-to-market on long-dated positions
Depended on the exchange's own warehouse receipt claims being accurate
Was not under FMC's derivatives oversight at the time

columns.label: Derivatives exchange (MCX, NCDEX)
points: Standardised futures and options contracts with defined expiry and settlement
Daily mark-to-market and margin collection from every participant
Clearing corporation guarantees every trade through novation
Directly regulated by SEBI, with position limits and surveillance

body.text: The label "exchange" is not a safety guarantee by itself. What matters is which regulator oversees it and what that regulator actually requires: guaranteed settlement, daily margining, and independent verification, not just a professional-looking trading screen.

children.text: SEBI's Toolkit for Commodity Derivatives Today
Since the 2015 merger, SEBI runs commodity derivatives with largely the same toolkit it uses for equity derivatives, plus a few tools unique to physical commodities:
Registration and surveillance.
Exchanges, clearing corporations and brokers all need SEBI registration, and trading activity is monitored for manipulation and cornering of positions.
Position limits.
Caps on how large a position any single client or entity can hold in a contract, meant to stop any one participant from dominating or squeezing a market, especially near expiry.
Margin norms.
Minimum margin requirements that rise automatically when a commodity gets more volatile, covered in full in the next chapter.
Price bands and circuit filters.
Daily limits on how far a contract's price can move, pausing trading if it is breached, similar in spirit to equity market circuit breakers.

markDefs.definition: A document issued by an accredited warehouse confirming that a specific quantity and quality of a commodity is stored there, which can be transferred to settle a futures contract by physical delivery.

children.text: Warehouse accreditation.

Physical delivery only works if the warehouse receipt behind it is trustworthy, which is precisely what NSEL got wrong. The Warehousing Development and Regulatory Authority (WDRA), set up under the Warehousing (Development and Regulation) Act, 2007, accredits warehouses and regulates
negotiable warehouse receipts
so that a receipt used to settle a futures contract actually means something.

body.label: Who checks the warehouse
body.value: WDRA-accredited warehouses, not the exchange itself
body.context: MCX and NCDEX rely on WDRA accreditation and independent assaying agencies to certify quality and quantity for commodities settled by physical delivery. This independent check is exactly what NSEL lacked.

body.title: Before you trade commodities, confirm these
steps: Your broker is a registered trading member of MCX and/or NCDEX, and your commodity trading account is separately activated (it is not automatically bundled with your equity account).
You are trading actual futures or options contracts on MCX/NCDEX, not a scheme that promises fixed returns from commodity trading.
You understand whether your contract settles in cash or by physical delivery, and what happens if you hold it into the delivery period.
If a platform ever claims 'guaranteed returns' from commodity trading, treat it as a red flag regardless of what exchange name it invokes.

cards.definition: The entity that guarantees settlement of every exchange trade by becoming the counterparty to both the buyer and the seller.
The process by which the clearing corporation legally substitutes itself as the counterparty to both sides of a matched trade.
A platform meant for near-immediate settlement of trades against real, currently held stock, as distinct from a derivatives exchange trading contracts for future settlement.
A regulatory cap on the maximum position size a single client or entity can hold in a contract.
The Warehousing Development and Regulatory Authority, which accredits warehouses and regulates negotiable warehouse receipts used in commodity delivery.
A transferable document certifying a specific quantity and quality of a commodity held in an accredited warehouse.

points: MCX and NCDEX are India's two demutualised, SEBI-regulated commodity derivatives exchanges. MCX leads in bullion, metals and energy; NCDEX leads in agricultural commodities.
The clearing corporation removes counterparty risk through novation: it becomes the legal counterparty to every buyer and every seller the moment a trade is matched.

NSEL's 2013 default happened because it operated as a lightly regulated spot exchange with unverified warehouse stock, not because commodity futures markets failed. It is a case study in why regulatory segment matters, not just the word 'exchange.'

Since the FMC merged into SEBI on 28 September 2015, SEBI applies registration requirements, position limits, margin norms, price bands and warehouse accreditation (via WDRA) to keep commodity derivatives markets orderly.
Before trading, confirm your broker's exchange membership is genuine and that you are trading standard exchange contracts, not an unregulated scheme borrowing an exchange's credibility.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Always verify a broker's exchange membership and SEBI registration independently before opening a commodity trading account.
